Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.

=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer-side assessment

The Seller’s “FINAL” labels and assertions that terms are settled or market-standard are negotiation positions, not evidence of agreement. The baseline is a AUD 24 million, debt-free/cash-free acquisition of 100% of Paperbark Analytics. On that basis, several proposals risk transferring substantial known or foreseeable value and execution risks to Wattlebridge. We should not accept them without checking the full SPA, schedules, due diligence and funds flow.

### 1. Price, debt and completion mechanics

**Riverlark facility — AUD 3.2 million outstanding.** The letter confirms the facility remains outstanding and no final security discharge is in the data room. A promise to provide a release after Completion leaves Wattlebridge exposed to debt and security over the acquired business after it has paid the price. That conflicts with a debt-free/cash-free deal.

**Push back:** require repayment at or before Completion from Seller proceeds (or another agreed source), together with lender payout evidence, an effective release of the security, and any required discharge filings. Make these completion deliverables and conditions to release of the purchase price. If a discharge filing necessarily follows Completion, require an irrevocable lender undertaking and a controlled funds flow that pays the lender directly; do not treat a post-Completion promise as sufficient.

**AUD 420,000 bonuses omitted from funds flow.** DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses, but the draft funds flow does not itemise them and the disclosure does not address payroll tax, superannuation or other on-costs. These may be transaction-related liabilities or employee entitlements, not an expense for Buyer to absorb unexpectedly.

**Push back:** identify the beneficiaries, conditions, gross amounts and on-costs; require the Seller to fund or pay them, with appropriate tax treatment and evidence. Ensure the completion accounts / price adjustment mechanics prevent double counting, and specifically address accrued bonuses and transaction expenses in the debt-free/cash-free definition. Consider a specific indemnity if the amounts or liabilities cannot be fully quantified before signing.

### 2. Conditions and third-party dependencies

**Bluefen — about 30% of FY26 revenue.** The documents say the change-of-control clause has conditions and that no final written consent or evidence of conditions being satisfied is included. “Reasonable endeavours” and treating the condition as satisfied on receipt of a consent letter are inadequate if the contract’s other conditions remain unfulfilled or the consent is qualified.

**Push back:** make effective, unconditional consent and satisfaction or waiver of every contractual condition a condition to Completion, with evidence in a form acceptable to Buyer. Include an outside date and a termination right if consent is not obtained. Do not deem the condition satisfied merely because a letter arrives. Given the revenue concentration, avoid completing first and bearing the risk of termination, renegotiation or service interruption.

**Other contracts.** DD-007 identifies a lease notification obligation, while DD-009 describes a restriction on assignment but does not say that a share sale itself requires consent. The Seller’s statements do not establish that no notice or consent is needed.

**Push back:** require a contract-by-contract review of change-of-control, assignment and notice provisions, including the lease and Mossvale arrangement. Require timely notices and any required consents as specified completion obligations or conditions. Do not overstate the documents as proving a consent is required where they do not; verify the operative contracts.

### 3. Warranties, caps, thresholds and time limits

**General cap of AUD 4.8 million (20% of price).** That may be inadequate for a AUD 24 million acquisition, particularly if the same cap also captures fundamental, title, tax or other high-value claims. The Seller’s assertion that 10–20% is “standard” does not establish that this allocation is suitable for this transaction.

**Push back:** seek a materially higher general warranty cap, calibrated to diligence findings and bargaining leverage. Keep separate, higher caps for tax and other specifically negotiated risks. Fundamental warranties—at least Seller capacity and authority, ownership of the shares, and title free of encumbrances—should have a substantially higher cap (potentially the price) and longer survival period, subject to appropriate enforceability advice. Consider separate treatment for fraud and deliberate concealment, which should not be protected by ordinary contractual limitations to the extent legally permissible.

**AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 tipping or deductible basket.** The proposed “only the excess above the basket” is a deductible basket: even after aggregate claims exceed AUD 250,000, the first AUD 250,000 remains unrecoverable. That leaves Buyer bearing meaningful losses before recovery begins. A per-claim de minimis may also exclude multiple related losses if drafted broadly.

**Push back:** seek a lower de minimis and a tipping basket, so that once qualifying claims exceed the basket, the full amount (not merely the excess) is recoverable. Ensure related claims are aggregated and that the de minimis does not defeat recovery for related claims or specific indemnities.

**18-month general warranty period and blanket limitation for all Claims.** An 18-month period may be too short for latent issues, especially tax, title, IP and matters requiring investigation. The proposal that limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise risks importing short periods into claims that need distinct treatment.

**Push back:** negotiate separate periods: a reasonable general warranty period; longer tax and fundamental periods aligned with applicable exposure and legal limitation periods; and specifically agreed periods for known risks. State clearly which limitation applies to each claim type. Require notice to describe the claim in reasonable detail and preserve claims notified within time, rather than requiring resolution or proceedings within that period.

**All limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to every Claim.** This could restrict contractual, indemnity and other remedies indiscriminately, including for specific risks, fraud, or deliberate misconduct.

**Push back:** define “Claims” and the scope of each limitation carefully. Preserve negotiated specific indemnities and any expressly agreed remedies from general warranty caps, baskets and time bars unless the parties intentionally agree otherwise. Review the operative drafting before accepting any exclusive-remedy or non-reliance clause; do not allow general language to override express warranties or agreed risk allocation.

### 4. Buyer knowledge and disclosure

**Buyer-knowledge exclusion.** The proposed exclusion reaches matters known by Buyer or its advisers, including matters discoverable in the data room or public records. “Discoverable” is especially broad: it can convert diligence access into a sweeping defence even where the Buyer did not actually know a matter or appreciate its significance.

**Push back:** limit any knowledge qualifier to the actual knowledge of specifically identified people, after reasonable inquiry, at a defined time. Exclude constructive or imputed knowledge based on what could have been found in the data room or public records. Preserve claims for breach of express warranties and specific indemnities unless a particular known matter is expressly priced and allocated.

**General data-room and public-register disclosure.** The Seller seeks to disclose every indexed data-room fact, the accounts, registers and public records, then provides specific disclosures that describe important gaps. That approach can make it difficult to identify what was actually disclosed against a warranty and may undermine meaningful warranty protection. The letter itself says the disclosed material does not establish several key facts.

**Push back:** reject blanket disclosure of the data room and public records. Require specific, fair disclosure against the relevant warranty, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the exception. Confirm the frozen data-room index and access record, but do not treat mere availability as disclosure or knowledge. The reservation that the Buyer must assess the facts does not cure an overbroad disclosure mechanism.

### 5. Specific identified risks

**Ironquay IP.** DD-004 says transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open, but is not independent verification of non-payment; there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment. The Seller’s existing indemnity, limited to a specific payment, may not secure ownership or usable rights in the materials.

**Push back:** require evidence of cleared payment and a confirmatory assignment or other effective transfer of all required IP rights, warranties as to ownership and non-infringement, and any necessary consents. If resolution before Completion is not possible, seek a specific indemnity covering the full consequences of missing, delayed or defective rights—including replacement, remediation and third-party claims—rather than limiting relief to the SOW3 payment. Check whether source code, deliverables, moral rights consents and supporting materials are covered.

**Export/privacy incident.** DD-006 describes a download link sent to an unintended external address and a possible 1,240 records, but does not establish access, scope, notification obligations or loss. Calling it preliminary does not eliminate the risk; nor should we assert it is a confirmed breach on this record.

**Push back:** require a complete investigation, preservation of evidence, access-log and recipient enquiries, assessment of applicable privacy and contractual notification obligations, and timely disclosure of new findings. Seek a specific indemnity for losses, remediation, investigation and notifications arising from the incident, with suitable cap and survival treatment, or another expressly negotiated protection. Consider making satisfactory resolution or a defined incident protocol a completion condition if the investigation reveals material exposure. Do not rely solely on a general warranty claim subject to the proposed low cap and short period.

**Supplier renewals — AUD 330,000 aggregate.** The Seller characterises three renewals as ordinary-course costs, but the disclosure does not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or ordinary course. Their related timing and scope should be read together.

**Push back:** obtain the executed contracts, renewal dates, termination rights, payment schedules and any accrued or committed amounts. Determine whether they are ordinary operating expenditure or debt-like / transaction-related liabilities under the price mechanics. Require accurate disclosure and ensure the same amounts are not both included in the price adjustment and recovered again under a claim.

**Tax.** “Settled under the general regime” is not enough. Tax liabilities can be latent and arise after Completion; the Seller offers no separate tax position in the materials.

**Push back:** require detailed tax warranties and a tax covenant or specific tax indemnity, with appropriate cap, survival period, conduct-of-claims protections and treatment of tax benefits. Review tax diligence before deciding scope.

### 6. Share title

DD-012 records Harbourglass as holder of 100% of issued shares, but the letter says this is only the source relied on and does not confirm Buyer verification. A register entry alone should not substitute for contractual protection and completion evidence.

**Push back:** require warranties that Seller owns and can transfer all shares, free of encumbrances, options and third-party rights; all necessary corporate approvals; and delivery at Completion of properly executed transfers, original certificates if issued, updated registers and other required corporate records. Apply fundamental-warranty caps and survival periods, not the general warranty regime.

## Recommendations in brief

Prioritise these points in the mark-up and negotiation:

1. **Protect the completion mechanics:** repay and discharge Riverlark at Completion; resolve the AUD 420,000 bonuses and associated on-costs in the funds flow and price mechanics.
2. **Make Bluefen consent effective:** require unconditional consent and satisfaction of all contractual conditions before Completion, with a termination right if unavailable.
3. **Reject broad risk compression:** negotiate a more adequate general cap, higher and longer protection for fundamental and tax matters, a tipping basket, and claim-specific time limits.
4. **Narrow knowledge and disclosure defences:** no constructive “discoverable” knowledge bar and no blanket data-room/public-record disclosure.
5. **Secure known-risk protections:** obtain effective Ironquay IP transfer; investigate and specifically allocate the privacy incident; verify supplier commitments and tax exposure.
6. **Verify title and other contract requirements:** obtain contractual title protection and completion evidence, and review the lease and Mossvale clauses rather than assuming either does—or does not—require consent.

These recommendations should be checked against the full SPA and transaction documents. The supplied materials state positions and disclose selected facts; they do not establish the final operative drafting, the full diligence record, or what the parties previously agreed.
